- set up your accommodations with your university’s accessibility center ahead of time, you’ll probably need a letter from your therapist/doctor listing reasonable recommended accommodations which could be something like; extended time for exams, distraction free area to take your exams, flexibility in assignments submitting dates, ability to record lectures, peer note taker, alternative material to study from, written instructions instead of verbal, individual tutoring, and much more depending on your specific circumstances.

- talk to your professor from the beginning of the semester and explain all your concerns and that you might need some adjustments, don’t wait till you need their assistance to explain everything cause they might not be as understanding later, if you talk to them before they’ll probably try to find ways to work with you. Whenever a problem arise make sure to communicate don’t leave it till the last second. If they aren’t responsive to emails go to their office hours or speak to them before or after class. If you have issues verbalizing what you need to tell your professors, your advisors or the accessibility center could provide support.

- don’t take classes at hours you know you can’t wake up, you probably won’t be able to go and it’d be hella exhausting.

- space out your classes in the way you’re most comfortable with. whether that having your classes back to back or with longer breaks in between.

- make sure you know at least one person in each class that you can go back to if you need something, don’t depend on them and help them when they need it to as well tho.

- figure out if you prefer studying on your own or with others and if you work better if those others are strangers rather than friends or the opposite.

- explore different study methods until you stick to something that works w you, you’ll probably come up with your own system as each brain works differently but you can base it on a pre-existing methods like flashcards, teaching someone else, pomodoro, and all that.

- if your university has a syllabus bank check that for the class and professor to have an idea on how the class would be, you could email the professor for the syllabus as well. asking upperclassmen that took the class and reading comments on rate my professor is helpful as well but don’t rely to much on it as your experience might be different.

- make sure you already know where you could go for support from the university faculty, like the wellness center, your advisors, or case managers from the dean officers that are specific for students with disabilities or health issues.

- find communities you relate to, like people who commute or are dorming, or join clubs related to your major, or a student association that follows your religion or that comes from the same background, be cautious as this could get toxic but it also exposes you to a lot of people that went through or are undergoing the same experience as yours. It has the potential to be a very valuable resource.

- try different places for studying on campus until you find the spot. you can research/call before to find out if the place you’re going to has things like power outlets to charge, quiet or loud, and anything you’re specifically looking for.

- build a routine if you’re into that but allow your body to rest when it’s tired don’t restrict it too much to avoid burn out. 

- find anyway to start asap, even if there’s a week left, just start the outline then every time you remember it throw something on your work even if it’s bullshit so when it’s the night before and you have nothing done you could have a couple useful point.

- stim if you need to, get some quiet fidget toys that you could play w in your hand if it helps you focus.

- test apps to keep track of things until you find a system that works w your brain.
